stories.title: Core inflation hits 3.3%, a Fed hike looks certain
chain: October core PCE rose 3.3% from a year earlier, above the 3.2% forecast
Headline PCE rose to 3.8% from 3.7%
A December Fed hike is now priced at roughly 92-98%, depending on the source
Higher rates for longer weigh most on expensive tech shares

depth.simple: The Fed's favourite inflation measure came in a little hotter than expected. Prices excluding food and energy were 3.3% higher than a year ago, against a forecast of 3.2%. The Fed wants 2%, so it is expected to raise interest rates again on 9 December. Higher rates make borrowing dearer and make shares that promise profits far in the future less attractive.
depth.standard: October core PCE was 3.3% year on year, slightly above the 3.2% consensus and described by some outlets as a three-year high. Headline PCE rose to 3.8% from 3.7%, in line with forecasts. Odds of a December hike were about 94% on Polymarket and 92-93% on Kalshi, with CME FedWatch readings between about 94% and 98%. The Fed meets on 8-9 December, and the November jobs report on 4 December is the last big data point before then. The US 10-year yield still eased 6bp to 4.85%.
depth.pro: A hike was already almost fully priced, so the surprise was small and the market reaction was muted: the 10-year yield fell 6bp, which suggests investors had expected something worse or are leaning on growth risk. The key variable is no longer December but the terminal rate and how long the Fed holds it. With headline inflation at 3.8%, the Fed cannot easily look through energy. Watch real yields, the 4 December jobs report, and whether long-duration equities keep trading as a rate-sensitive factor.

depth.simple: On Wednesday the US market had a scary morning and an almost calm finish. The S&P 500 was down more than 3% at one point, then bought back nearly all of it. That does not mean the worry is gone. It means buyers are active at low prices while sellers are still nervous about AI spending, tariffs and interest rates.
depth.standard: The S&P 500 closed at 7,182.78 (-0.25%), the Nasdaq Composite at 23,585.80 (-0.62%) and the Dow at 50,182.95 (+0.33%), its second close above 50,000. Intraday the S&P 500 fell as much as 3.2% and the Nasdaq as much as 4.6%; the Nasdaq 100 briefly touched 20% below its October closing peak. Advancers beat decliners 370 to 128 in the S&P 500, and small and mid-sized shares did better. Nvidia fell about 3.9%, with Oracle and Micron also lower. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index had already dropped 7.88% on Tuesday.
depth.pro: A 3% intraday drawdown with a near-full recovery looks like forced selling and a liquidity air pocket followed by dip-buying, helped by thin pre-holiday trading. Breadth of 370 to 128 on the close shows rotation out of mega-cap AI rather than a broad exit. The touch of a 20% Nasdaq 100 drawdown is a technical marker some systematic funds watch. Thursday's US closure and Friday's early close mean the next real test of this bounce comes with thin volume.

stories.title: US proposes new tariffs on 14 economies
chain: The USTR proposed new Section 301 tariffs on 14 trading partners
Reports say rates of up to 15% for the EU and Japan and up to 20% for China, but details are unconfirmed
European exporters and shares sold off, with the Euro Stoxx 50 down 1.82%
Implementation may only start in January, so the final rates are still open

depth.simple: The US government proposed new import taxes on goods from 14 countries and regions, including the EU. Nothing is final: reports disagree on the exact rates and the start date. Shares in Europe fell anyway, because investors worry that companies selling to the US will earn less.
depth.standard: The US Trade Representative proposed new Section 301 tariffs on 14 economies. Reports differ: one says up to 20% on China and 15% on the EU and Japan; another says the 15% cap covers the EU, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, that Mexico is temporarily exempt, and that implementation is delayed until January. European shares fell: the Stoxx 600 lost 1.06%, the DAX 1.26%, the IBEX 35 2.0% and the Euro Stoxx 50 1.82%. The euro gained 0.5% against the dollar.
depth.pro: A proposal and a comment period leave room for negotiation, so markets are pricing a probability-weighted outcome rather than a rate. The hit lands on EU autos, machinery and chips, and adds to an inflation picture where core PCE is already 3.3%: tariffs push the Fed and the ECB toward tighter policy, not looser. The euro's rise despite weak equities suggests the market read the tariffs as hurting the US price level. Watch the comment deadlines, any exemptions, and whether the EU prepares a response.

Asian shares steadied, with Nikkei and Kospi up modestly in the data file

depth.simple: South Korea's stock market fell about 6% on Wednesday because investors dumped chip makers such as Samsung and SK Hynix. On Thursday the country's central bank raised interest rates to fight inflation, and markets calmed a little. Korea's economy depends heavily on chips, so its market swings a lot when AI shares move.
depth.standard: The Kospi closed at 4,697.51 on Wednesday, down 308.52 points, and the Nikkei lost 2.7% as Nvidia's fall hit chip stocks. On Thursday the Bank of Korea raised its base rate 25bp to 3.25%, the highest since late 2024, in a 5-2 vote, with inflation at 2.8% against a 2% target. It raised its 2026 and 2027 growth forecasts to 3.9% and 4.1%. Thursday's data shows the Nikkei up 0.75% and the Kospi up 0.28%. Early reports had larger gains in Tokyo and Seoul and in Taiwan, but the data file is the figure used here.
depth.pro: The Kospi is effectively a leveraged proxy for two memory names, so it amplifies the AI-capex trade in both directions: -6% on Wednesday and a rebound the day after the BoK hike. A central bank tightening into a chip sell-off shows that inflation, not equity weakness, is driving policy across Asia. Watch the won, foreign flows into Samsung and SK Hynix, and whether the BoK's signal of more hikes spreads to Japan and Taiwan.

stories.title: Iran says two more tankers hit mines in Hormuz
chain: Iran's Revolutionary Guards said two tankers hit mines and caught fire on Wednesday
Earlier this week it reported three more, a claim not independently confirmed
Brent rose on Wednesday, then fell 3.94% to $90.88 on Thursday
Oil stays caught between supply fears and a forecast surplus

depth.simple: Iran says two more oil tankers hit sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway many oil shipments use. These claims come from Iran's own forces and are hard to check. Oil prices jumped on Wednesday and then fell back on Thursday, which shows traders are unsure how much oil is really being blocked.
depth.standard: The Revolutionary Guards Navy said two tankers hit naval mines and caught fire on 25 November, after three others earlier in the week. The account rests mainly on one report and has not been independently corroborated. Tanker tracker Kpler reportedly showed lower crude flows out of the Gulf, and Houthi forces reportedly targeted a Saudi refinery. Brent was about $94.61 on Wednesday and fell 3.94% to $90.88 in Thursday's data; WTI is at $84.12 (+0.53%).
depth.pro: The market is trading the gap between headline risk and physical flows: a forecast fourth-quarter surplus caps the rally while each mine report adds a risk premium that fades without confirmed outages. Brent falling 3.94% on a day of fresh attacks suggests traders fade unverified claims. The second-order link is inflation: with headline PCE at 3.8%, an oil spike would push the Fed further. Watch Kpler flow data, insurance rates for Gulf transits, and any US naval response.

stories.title: AI rebound fades: Nvidia -6.6%, Nasdaq -1.5%
chain: Monday's relief rally had not fixed the doubts about AI spending
Nvidia fell about 6.6% and AMD about 9% after a large share resale filing
Tech was the weakest sector and the Nasdaq lost 1.48%, while the Dow rose 0.85%
The S&P 500 closed at 7,201.09, its eighth loss in nine sessions

depth.simple: Monday's big bounce did not last. On Tuesday, shares in chip and AI companies fell again, and the Nasdaq lost almost 1.5%. Money moved towards steadier sectors such as health care and consumer goods, so the Dow still rose. It shows investors are still nervous about how much is being spent on AI, and about who will pay for it.
depth.standard: The S&P 500 closed at 7,201.09 (-0.50%), the Nasdaq Composite at 23,733.54 (-1.48%) and the Dow at 50,018.70 (+0.85%). Nvidia gave back about 6.6% after Monday's 31% jump. AMD fell about 9% after a filing that lets holders resell around 337 million shares. Technology was the weakest sector; health care, staples and communications rose, helped by Conference Board consumer confidence that beat forecasts. Monday's rally had recovered only part of the previous week's 10% Nasdaq fall.
depth.pro: Monday looked like short covering, and Tuesday shows it lacked follow-through: leadership rotated from high-beta semis to defensives and value, which is what a market does when it still wants to de-risk. The AMD resale filing adds supply overhang, the Nvidia SEC question is unresolved, and Wednesday's PCE is the next test of the rate path. Watch the semiconductor index against its Monday low, volatility, and whether equal-weight indexes keep outperforming.

depth.standard: ANT fell 6.5% to $81.91, according to Bloomberg, Axios and CNBC, after trading as low as about $76 during the day. depth.pro: A break of the offer price in the fourth session removes the underwriters' easy narrative and invites a test of whether the bank stabilisation bid is working. The stock is trading with the AI factor rather than on its own news, so index-level semis moves matter more than company events. Watch volume near $83, analyst initiations as quiet periods end, and the supply of shares from early holders as lock-ups approach.

stories.title: Nvidia soars 31% as Jensen Huang returns as CEO
chain: Huang resigned on 12 Nov after reports about his private life and a China spy link
Nvidia's board voted unanimously to reinstate him, after input from the US government
Nvidia shares jumped about 31% in a day
The SEC accounting probe and the board's own investigation are still open

depth.simple: Nvidia's boss, Jensen Huang, quit about two weeks ago after news stories about his private life. On Monday the board brought him back. Investors cheered: the share price rose almost a third in a day. But the questions have not gone away. Reuters reported that the US market regulator, the SEC, is looking at how Nvidia does its accounting, and the board says its own investigation will continue.
depth.standard: Nvidia's board voted unanimously to reinstate Huang as president, CEO and director. It said it received input from senior levels of the US government and is confident his return poses no national security risk; reports say President Trump urged the move. Nvidia closed up about 31%, a gain of roughly $950 billion in market value, and led the whole market higher. Reuters reported that SEC staff are examining the company's accounting, reportedly including how revenue is classified by region and customer-payment guarantees. It was not clear on Monday whether the probe changed, and the board's committee will finish its investigation.
depth.pro: The move prices out key-man and governance risk, not the accounting question. A 31% gain on a mega-cap implies the prior 14% drop was largely positioning and liquidity. What remains is event risk with long tails: SEC findings on revenue geography and customer guarantees, any DOJ follow-up, export-control politics and political dependence on Washington's goodwill. Watch Nvidia's weight in index funds, options positioning after a record move, and whether suppliers and AI-capex peers keep their share of the bounce.

Williams ruled out a jumbo hike on 17 Nov and stressed data dependence, so the core PCE print mostly moves the 2027 path and the terminal rate. A hot number would tighten financial conditions just as equities are fragile; a soft one would hand the bounce a second leg. depth.simple: Oil got cheaper on Monday even though Iran said three more ships hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz, a key shipping route. Two things pulled the price down: the US seems willing to give talks more time, and there is more oil being produced than the world needs. That is good news for Europe, which pays a lot for energy.
depth.standard: Brent fell 3.46% to $89.37 and WTI 4.54% to $80.17. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said three tankers caught fire after hitting naval mines; the claim is not independently verified. Trump signalled more time for diplomacy while saying he could resume the war next year if talks fail, and the US naval blockade continues. The IEA expects a surplus this quarter, Libya's Sharara pipeline has reopened and October inventories rose by 52 million barrels, according to Deutsche Bank.
depth.pro: The market is treating Hormuz headlines as noise against a physical surplus: with the strait effectively closed, the glut is coming from elsewhere and demand destruction. Eurasia Group sees Brent in the lower half of $80-100. The tail risk is a diplomatic collapse or mine incidents that stop escorted traffic, which could move prices fast. For the ECB, lower oil eases the energy-inflation argument at the margin.

depth.simple: Shares fell hard again on Friday. The S&P 500 is now more than 10% below its record high from 6 October. Traders call that a correction. The tech-heavy Nasdaq fell over 5% in one day and is now lower than where it started the year. For the whole week the Nasdaq lost 10%, its worst week since March 2020. Futures point to a bounce on Monday, but nobody knows if it will last.

The S&P 500 is more than 10% below its 6 October record, the usual definition of a correction. Reports tie the drop to AI-spending worries, a plunge in chip stocks and hawkish comments from Fed officials, including Philadelphia Fed president Anna Paulson, who said rates need to rise again. US stock futures were about 2% higher early on Monday.
depth.pro: A move of this size in a week points to forced selling and falling liquidity, not a slow re-pricing. Concentration is the amplifier: when the biggest AI names fall 13-14% in a day, index-level losses follow even if rates are calm. The 10-year yield fell 14bp, so this is an equity-risk-premium and positioning shock, not a rates shock. Watch whether the Monday futures bounce holds, volatility term structure, margin calls in Asia, and whether credit spreads start to widen.

Single-stock events at this weight pass straight into the index and into options and dealer positioning. On Monday South Korea's market dropped almost 6% at one point, which paused some automatic selling, before settling down about 3%. Governments in Taiwan, China and South Korea announced measures to calm things. For Spain the damage was smaller: the IBEX 35 fell 1.63%.

depth.simple: A narrow sea lane in the Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz, is where a large share of the world's oil ships pass. Two more tankers were hit there. Iran says it will keep it closed until its demands are met, and Qatar is trying to broker talks. Oil rose only slightly to $92.57 because forecasts of extra supply are holding prices back.
depth.standard: Brent closed at $92.57, up 0.64%, and WTI at $83.98, up 0.93%. UKMTO reported two tankers hit by projectiles in the Strait. Iran's foreign minister has said the strait will not reopen until its demands are met, and Qatar is reported to be mediating. The US blockade continues. Trackers disagree on how much oil is moving: one counts only two transits on 15 Nov against a pre-crisis 85 a day, another says shipments have not been interrupted. Brent is far below last month's high of $117.34.
depth.pro: The market is pricing the physical risk lightly because stock draws are offset by weak demand expectations and an IEA surplus forecast. The risk is asymmetric: a sudden insurance or access shock moves prompt spreads before it moves flat price. For Europe, higher gas and oil feed inflation and the ECB's path. Watch tanker transit data, war-risk insurance, Qatar mediation headlines and any change to the US blockade.

stories.title: Hormuz stays tense, yet Brent holds near $92

depth.simple: The danger around the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow sea route for much of the world's oil, has not gone away. Ships have been hit and the US is blocking Iranian ports. But oil prices did not jump, because the world is expected to have more oil than it needs. Brent finished almost unchanged at about $92 a barrel.
depth.standard: Brent closed at $91.98 (+0.03%) and WTI at $83.21 (-0.06%). Iran said two more tankers hit sea mines on Thursday; those claims come mainly from Iranian sources and are not independently confirmed. The US says it is blockading Iran's Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman ports, a third US carrier has arrived, and a Senate war powers resolution failed 48-51. Trump reportedly said he is not rushing a decision. An ADNOC vessel was attacked, with 11 crew injured and one missing.
depth.pro: The market is pricing physical balances (a Q4 surplus and US stock builds) over tail risk, so escalation would show first in war-risk insurance, freight and the Brent time spreads rather than spot. A slow political timeline (decision after the new year) reduces near-term event risk but leaves the strait exposed to incidents. For Europe, lower oil lessens energy-driven inflation and eases pressure on the ECB.

depth.simple: The US government said companies now need a licence to send advanced AI chips to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand. It also limits Chinese firms from renting that computing power remotely through foreign data centres. The aim is to stop China getting chips through the back door. For Nvidia, it adds another worry on top of its leadership crisis.
depth.standard: The Commerce Department's interim rule covers exports and re-exports of advanced semiconductors to the five countries, and overseas data centres that give Chinese firms access to such chips now need federal licences. Operators already providing that capacity get 90 days after the rule takes effect to apply. Coverage links the move to the Nvidia scandal and to an upcoming meeting between Trump and Xi. Nvidia shares fell on the news. Some details of the Huang story rest on a few outlets and are still unsettled.
depth.pro: The significant change is the remote-access provision: it targets compute-as-a-service, not just hardware shipments, which is how a lot of China-linked demand had been routed through Southeast Asian data centres. Watch for how Nvidia sizes the revenue at risk on tonight's call, how Singapore- and Malaysia-based operators apply for licences, and whether Beijing retaliates around the Trump–Xi talks. Second-order effects hit server makers and memory suppliers in Asia, which fits this week's weakness in Kospi chip names.

stories.title: Nvidia loses its founder-CEO days before earnings
chain: Huang exits after a board probe
Leadership and China-security questions
Chip stocks sold worldwide
This week's earnings become a confidence test

depth.simple: Jensen Huang, who founded Nvidia and ran it for over 30 years, left as CEO last week after a board investigation into his personal conduct, which included reports that he was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. Nvidia makes the chips behind most of the world's AI, so investors treat it as the barometer for the whole AI trade. Losing its leader just before it reports results pushed investors to sell chip stocks from New York to Seoul.
depth.standard: The board named CFO Colette Kress interim CEO and created an independent chair role, filled by Harvey Jones. The official wording is a resignation; CNBC's sources say the board pushed him out, and today report that the board is not considering bringing him back despite a petition and allies lobbying for it. Congressional committees may call him to testify. Nvidia had its worst week since the April 2025 tariff selloff, and the selling hit its Asian suppliers this morning: SK Hynix −7.9%, Kospi −3.6%. Monday's US session opened lower again, with Nasdaq 100 futures down; closing levels were still provisional in the sources we checked.
depth.pro: Two things drive the valuation question. First, key-person risk: Huang personally anchored the hyperscaler relationships and the credibility of the product roadmap. Second, a possible national-security angle that could tighten scrutiny of China-linked sales. Q3 consensus EPS is about $2.47–2.49. The quarter itself is largely locked in by orders already placed, so the market will trade the guidance and whether Kress can reassure on roadmap and customer commitments. A beat with soft guidance would likely be read as the start of a de-rating.

stories.title: The US 10-year yield breaks 5% as a December hike gets priced in
chain: October inflation runs hot (+0.4% m/m)
~92% odds of a Fed hike on 9 Dec
10-year yield: 4.86% → 5.15% in a week
Costlier borrowing, pressure on stock valuations

depth.simple: US inflation came in higher than expected in October, mostly because of energy. That makes it very likely the Federal Reserve raises interest rates again in December, after already raising them in September. When investors expect higher rates, government bond yields rise too. The 10-year US yield is the reference rate for mortgages and company borrowing around the world, and it is now above 5%. At that level, safe bonds become a serious alternative to stocks.
depth.standard: The Fed's range is 3.75–4.00% after a September hike under Chair Kevin Warsh and a hold on 28 October, when two members voted to hike. Futures price about 92% odds of +0.25 pts at the 8–9 December meeting and 8% odds of +0.50. Governor Waller has floated the bigger move. Warsh speaks today and the October minutes come out Wednesday. Stocks still rose on the week (S&P +2.5%), but fast-growing tech stocks are the most exposed if yields keep climbing, because more of their value sits in profits far in the future.
depth.pro: The 10-year added roughly 30bp in a week to about 5.15%. Core CPI has printed +0.3% m/m three months running, about 3.7% annualised, so the debate is the terminal rate, not the timing. Watch the term premium: if long yields keep rising after hikes are already priced, the driver is fiscal and supply worries rather than Fed expectations, which is worse for equity multiples. Note that the BLS did not publish a 12-month CPI rate because October 2025 data were never collected during the shutdown.

stories.title: Iran escalates in the Gulf: drones at Bahrain, tankers hit in Hormuz
chain: IRGC drones at a US radar site in Bahrain
Iran says 6 tankers hit since Sunday
Shipping risk up, but glut fears cap oil
Expensive energy keeps inflation sticky

depth.simple: Iran launched drones at a US military site in Bahrain over the weekend; Bahrain says it shot them all down. Iran also says several oil tankers were hit by mines or projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow channel that normally carries about a fifth of the world's oil. Oil is already expensive, with Brent around $96 a barrel, and that feeds the inflation pushing central banks to raise rates.
depth.standard: Iran has restricted passage through Hormuz and attacks ships it says break its rules. The UK's maritime agency (UKMTO) confirmed one vessel was hit, with all crew safe; Iran's claim that a supertanker sank is unverified. Reuters reports President Trump is weighing holding off on strikes unless there are new provocations. Oil actually eased this morning because the IEA's outlook revived worries about a global supply surplus, so the market is weighing disruption against weak demand.
depth.pro: Watch the oil futures curve and tanker rates rather than headline Brent: a real disruption shows up as steeper backwardation and a spike in freight. The second-order effect matters more. European gas has risen and Japan's Q3 contraction was blamed on energy costs, so energy is now a growth problem for importers (Europe, Japan, Korea) and an inflation problem for the Fed and the ECB at once. That stagflationary mix is the worst backdrop for long-duration equities.

stories.title: Anthropic lists this week: the biggest test yet of AI appetite
chain: 825M shares at $70–78
Raises up to ~$64B, the largest IPO ever
Prices Wed 18, trades Thu 19 (ANT)
The first-day move is a vote on AI valuations
stories.disclosure: This brief is written by Claude, which is made by Anthropic. It covers Anthropic like any other company and takes no view on buying the shares.

depth.simple: Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI models, plans to list its shares on the Nasdaq this week. It wants to raise around $61–64 billion, which would make it by far the largest stock market debut ever. How the shares trade on day one will show how much investors still want to pay for AI right after the Nvidia shock.
depth.standard: Pricing is expected Wednesday 18 November, with trading from Thursday 19 November under the ticker ANT. The range values the company at up to about $1.4 trillion fully diluted, below the roughly $2 trillion some investors talked about over the summer. Reports say the banks are weighing a higher price, which would push the valuation to $1.5 trillion or more. Some analysts read the lower range as a deliberate choice to leave room for a first-day jump. Reports also say demand is strong (one outlet says the book is several times covered) and that Nvidia plans to invest up to $10 billion in Anthropic ahead of the listing; sources differ on the raise size ($64B to $80B) and valuation ($1.3–1.5T).
depth.pro: Mind the share count. On about 13.1B basic shares the market cap is roughly $0.92–1.02T; the $1.3–1.4T headline includes options and restricted stock. A $60B+ raise is also a liquidity event: funds may trim other mega-cap AI holdings to make room, a supply overhang for the sector in the week it lists. For the medium-term price, lock-up expiries matter more than day one.

stories.title: Europe at records while Asia slides: the AI selloff is uneven
chain: Stoxx 600 record close, best week since June
Led by insurers and oil majors, not tech
Asia today: Kospi −3.6%, Nikkei −2.4%
Europe's low AI exposure works as a shelter

depth.simple: European stocks closed at another record on Friday and the IBEX 35 stayed above 20,000, while Asian markets fell hard this morning. The difference is what each market is made of. Korea and Taiwan are full of chipmakers that sell to Nvidia. Europe's indexes are heavy in banks, insurers and energy companies, which do fine when rates are high and oil is expensive.
depth.standard: The Stoxx 600 closed at 664.14, up 2.4% on the week, led by insurers and oil producers while chipmakers lagged (Infineon −4.3%). In Japan, data showed the economy contracted in the third quarter as energy costs bit, pulling the Nikkei down 2.4%. Euro-area inflation reached 4.0% in October, and most economists expect the ECB to raise its deposit rate in December as well.
depth.pro: Sector mix explains most of the gap. Europe is overweight financials, which earn more from lending when rates rise, and energy, and it is underweight semiconductors. The cushion has limits: an ECB hike into slowing growth and energy-led inflation is a stagflation setup, and the IBEX's heavy bank weighting makes it sensitive to any credit wobble. Korea and Taiwan's concentration in SK Hynix, Samsung and TSMC makes their indexes leveraged bets on AI spending.
